keyVerseText: And Joseph saw Ephraim's children of the third generation: the children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were brought up upon Joseph's knees. brought: Heb. born
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מָכִיר (Mâkîyr) derives from the root מָכַר (mâkar), which means 'to sell.' This root encompasses the idea of selling literally, such as merchandise or persons, and figuratively, such as surrendering. The name מָכִיר thus carries the connotation of one who is associated with selling or a salesman, reflecting a transactional or relational dynamic embedded in its etymology beyond the simple English transliteration as a proper name.
usageInScripture: The word מָכִיר appears 22 times in Scripture, primarily as a proper name referring to two individuals: the eldest son of Manasseh and a son of Ammiel. The dominant translation, 'of Machir,' occurs 12 times, indicating a possessive or familial relationship. Other translations such as 'and Machir,' 'unto Machir,' and 'out of Machir' show its consistent use as a personal name linked to lineage or tribal identity, emphasizing the importance of family heritage and tribal leadership in the biblical narrative.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מָכִיר as a name rooted in the concept of selling invites reflection on God's providence in the lineage and tribes of Israel, where even names connected to commerce or exchange carry divine purpose. Machir, as a progenitor of a large family and a tribal leader, symbolizes God's faithfulness in establishing and preserving His covenant people. This highlights the sovereignty of God over human history and genealogy, affirming that every individual and family line has a role in His redemptive plan. Recognizing the name's origin enriches our appreciation of biblical characters as part of God's unfolding story of salvation.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 50:23 states, 'And Joseph saw Ephraim's children of the third generation: the children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were brought up upon Joseph's knees.' Here, the mention of Machir connects the narrative to the continuation of God's covenant promises through the descendants of Manasseh. The word מָכִיר anchors the verse in a familial and tribal context, emphasizing the nurturing and blessing of future generations. It reminds us that God's faithfulness extends through families and that the legacy of faith is passed down, sustained by His providential care.
